metadata.file_name: 114. Khoudi et al. (2024). Identifying the contextual factors related to the reading performance of Moroccan fourth-grade students from a Machine Learning-based Approach..pdf
metadata.title: Identifying the contextual factors related to the reading performance of Moroccan fourth-grade students from a Machine Learning-based Approach.

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2016 Morocco grade-4 microdata merged across student, teacher, and school files via IEA IDB Analyzer (v5.0). The manuscript describes extensive variable cleaning (dropping ID/weight/maintenance variables, removing benchmark/PV variables, and excluding variables with >10% missingness) and then trains supervised classifiers on the resulting dataset (n=5446). No PIRLS sampling/replicate weight variables (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight procedures (BRR/jackknife) are reported as being applied in model estimation. Given the use of standard ML classifiers (e.g., Gradient Boosting, Random Forest, SVM), the paper does not document a complex-survey-weighted estimation strategy, so results should be interpreted as conditional on the analytic sample rather than explicitly population-representative estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not used as the dependent variable: PIRLS provides 5 plausible values for reading, but the authors convert them into a single majority-vote benchmark-based reading proficiency class (Low vs Others) and then model that binary outcome. Missing data handling is implemented via SimpleImputer, which replaces missing values with mode values for categorical variables (and effectively mean/mode-style imputation depending on variable type), so a PV-specific missing-data strategy is not applicable to the outcome construction.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PIRLS 2016 Morocco grade-4 student, teacher, and school data merged in IDB Analyzer (v5.0). Started from 5489 entries, removed 43 tied cases after combining PV-based benchmark variables via majority vote, yielding 5446 students. Dropped 192 of 486 initial merged variables (IDs/weights/maintenance/redundant variables; removed 22 numerical scale index variables; removed 30 benchmark variables and PVs except the newly created ASRIBM response benchmark). Excluded variables with missing rates >10% and then imputed remaining missing values using SimpleImputer while retaining all 5446 observations.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Gradient Boosting (best): Accuracy=80.97, F1=63.80. Other models: Random Forest Accuracy=79.38 F1=56.40; Logistic Regression Accuracy=78.79 F1=62.76; KNN Accuracy=75.89 F1=48.70; Naive Bayes Accuracy=73.01 F1=60.73; Decision Tree Accuracy=73.50 F1=52.37; SVM Accuracy=70.20 (F1 not reported/0.00).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 Reading (Morocco) the study leveraged Reading achievement too low, Students confident in reading, Early literacy tasks, Student age, and Reading is boring to predict whether students fall in the Low reading proficiency class versus Others, finding that Gradient Boosting achieved the highest classification performance (Accuracy=80.97, F1=63.80). This indicates that combining early literacy competence with students’ reading self-beliefs and classroom/school learning climate variables may improve identification of students at risk of low reading achievement, though the study’s binary outcome is derived from PV-based benchmarks and the paper does not document survey-weighted estimation or causal identification.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PIRLS 2016 Morocco grade-4 reading data (n=5446) and constructs a binary outcome indicating whether a student is at the “Low” reading benchmark level versus “Others,” derived from PIRLS PV-based benchmark variables using majority vote. After merging student, teacher, and school questionnaires in IDB Analyzer, the authors reduce the variable set (dropping IDs/weights/maintenance, removing most benchmark/PV variables, and excluding variables with >10% missingness) and impute remaining missing values with SimpleImputer. Seven supervised classifiers are compared using a 7:3 train/test split with stratification by the response benchmark; Gradient Boosting performs best with Accuracy=80.97 and F1=63.80 (Random Forest: Accuracy=79.38, F1=56.40). The top predictors highlighted by Gradient Boosting feature importance include early literacy tasks, reading confidence, parental commitment, and school emphasis on academic success. Limitations include lack of reported complex-survey weighting/replicate-weight use and the fact that the model is predictive rather than causal.
